reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An acromelic dysplasia with severe short stature, very short hands and feet, and stiff joints, but generally a milder systemic course than geleophysic dysplasia
Caused by heterozygous variants in a specific region of FBN1, the fibrillin-1 gene, and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
Facial features include a well-proportioned round face, sometimes with subtle fullness, without the marked storage-like appearance of a mucopolysaccharidosis
Cardiac valve and airway involvement is much less prominent than in geleophysic dysplasia, which is the key clinical distinction
Radiographs show short tubular bones, cone-shaped epiphyses, and an internal notch of the femoral head can be a helpful sign
Intelligence is typically normal and life expectancy is usually preserved
Management is supportive, centred on growth monitoring and orthopaedic care for joint limitation
reference.pathophysiology: Acromicric dysplasia is caused by variants clustering in a particular domain of FBN1, the same gene implicated in Marfan syndrome and in the dominant form of geleophysic dysplasia, but the effect here disturbs the microfibril-TGF-beta axis in a way that favours short, dense bones rather than the tall, lax Marfan phenotype. Altered fibrillin-1 microfibril function dysregulates transforming growth factor beta signalling in connective tissue and cartilage, producing acromelic shortening, joint stiffness, and thickened but relatively unaffected visceral structures compared with the more severe geleophysic form.
additionalInvestigations: FBN1 analysis, typically within a skeletal dysplasia gene panel
Skeletal survey to demonstrate short tubular bones and cone-shaped epiphyses
Echocardiography to assess for and monitor any valvular involvement
Airway assessment where respiratory symptoms are present
Growth monitoring with plotting on appropriate charts
redFlags: Emerging cardiac valve disease that would suggest overlap with geleophysic dysplasia
Any airway narrowing or respiratory compromise
Features suggesting an alternative, more systemically aggressive dysplasia
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good with normal intelligence and life expectancy in most cases, as the serious cardiac and airway complications of geleophysic dysplasia are usually absent, though short stature and joint stiffness persist.
pitfalls: Confusing it with geleophysic dysplasia and either over- or under-estimating cardiac risk
Mistaking the phenotype for a mucopolysaccharidosis and pursuing enzyme testing unnecessarily
Overlooking the FBN1 basis and its distinction from Marfan syndrome when counselling
Assuming short stature will respond to growth hormone without evidence of benefit

management: No specific pharmacotherapy is available; management is supportive, directed at the short stature and joint stiffness of this FBN1-related dysplasia
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain joint mobility and manage progressive contractures and stiff hands
Orthopaedic review of joint contractures and any limb deformity
Echocardiographic surveillance for valvular involvement, which is usually mild but should be monitored
Airway assessment where respiratory symptoms arise, distinguishing the milder course from geleophysic dysplasia
Serial growth monitoring plotted on appropriate charts through a multidisciplinary skeletal dysplasia and genetics service
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance, with family screening
